DESCRIPTIVE NOTE ON KUTCH WILDLIFE SANCTUARY
(Position as on 01/01/2023)

1. INTRODUCTION AND LEGAL STATUS

Kutch Wildlife Sanctuary is one of the smaller protected areas in the Kachchh district, notified primarily to conserve the arid and semi-arid grassland and scrub ecosystem typical of the region. The sanctuary falls within the jurisdiction of Kutch Wildlife Range, Kachchh (West) Wildlife Division. The final notification under Section 26(A) of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, was issued vide Notification No. WLP/1086/84/1532 dated 11/09/1986. The sanctuary is managed with the primary objective of protecting the chinkara (Indian gazelle) and its habitat, while also providing a secure area for the Indian wolf, desert fox, and various resident and migratory birds.

2. GEOGRAPHICAL LOCATION AND BOUNDARIES

The sanctuary is situated in the western part of Kachchh district, approximately 45 km west of Bhuj town. The area lies between 23°10' N and 23°25' N latitude and 69°30' E and 69°45' E longitude. The sanctuary is bounded on the north by revenue wasteland and scrubland, on the east by agricultural fields of the villages of Nirona and Kotay, on the south by the seasonal riverbed and grazing land, and on the west by the boundary of the adjoining revenue village. The boundary pillars are numbered from KP-1 to KP-118 and are maintained by the Range staff.

The terrain is generally flat to gently undulating, with scattered low hills and depressions. The highest point within the sanctuary is near the central-eastern side, rising to about 150 m above mean sea level. The general slope is towards the south-west, where the drainage converges into a seasonal nullah that flows out of the sanctuary during heavy rainfall years. The soil is predominantly sandy loam with patches of clay in the low-lying areas and gravelly soil on the elevated tracts.

**Subject: Revised Guidelines for Wildlife Rescue and Rehabilitation Operations – Implementation and Compliance**

In supersession of all previous circulars on the subject, the following comprehensive guidelines are hereby issued for the standardised handling of wildlife rescue, first-aid, transportation, and rehabilitation across all territorial and sanctuary divisions under the Wildlife Circle, Bhuj. These protocols take effect from 1 February 2026, with a mandatory training period for all field staff during the last fortnight of January 2026.

**1. Scope and Applicability**

1.1 These guidelines apply to all forest personnel, including Range Forest Officers (RFOs), Deputy Conservators of Forests (DCFs), veterinary officers, and temporary staff engaged in rescue operations.

1.2 The provisions cover all wild fauna, including reptiles, birds, and mammals, found within the territorial jurisdiction of the Wildlife Circle, Bhuj. They do not apply to domestic livestock or companion animals, which remain under the purview of the District Animal Husbandry Department.

1.3 All rescue operations shall be conducted in accordance with the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, as amended, and the Standing Orders of the Chief Wildlife Warden, Gujarat State.

**2. Reporting and Initial Response**

2.1 Any information regarding a wild animal in distress, conflict, or requiring intervention shall be recorded in the prescribed format (Form R-1) at the nearest Forest Range Office. The form shall be entered in the daily diary maintained at each range.

2.2 Upon receipt of a complaint, the RFO or his designated subordinate shall verify the information within two hours of receipt during daylight hours. For night-time complaints, verification shall commence at first light unless the situation is assessed as an emergency.

2.3 Emergency situations, including but not limited to snakebite incidents, animal attacks on humans, or animals trapped in wells, shall be reported immediately by phone to the Divisional Forest Officer (DFO) and the nearest veterinary officer on duty. The phone report shall be followed by a written report within 24 hours.

2.4 All complaints, whether attended or not, shall be logged in a centralised register at the range level. The register shall be open for inspection by the DCF during all supervisory visits.

**3. Rescue Team Composition and Equipment**

3.1 Each division shall maintain a minimum of one fully equipped rescue kit at the division headquarters and one at each range headquarters. The kit shall include, but not be limited to:

a) Catch poles of varying lengths (6 ft, 10 ft, and 14 ft)
b) Snake tongs and snake tubes (three sizes)
c) Heavy-duty gloves, leather gauntlets, and safety goggles
d) Cloth bags, gunny bags, and ventilated transport crates
e) Ropes, nets, and hooks for well rescues
f) First-aid kit comprising antiseptics, bandages, splints, and saline
g) Torch, headlamps, and spare batteries
h) Mobile phone with emergency contact numbers pre-programmed

3.2 The rescue team shall consist of at least three trained personnel for mammal rescues and at least two trained personnel for reptile rescues. No rescue operation shall be undertaken by a single individual.

3.3 All personnel involved in rescue operations shall undergo a two-day refresher training at the division headquarters once every six months. The first such training under these guidelines shall be completed by 30 June 2026.

---

**1. CLINICAL EXAMINATION (12/01/2024)**

- **Temperature:** 38.9°C (rectal)
- **Pulse:** 112/min, weak, regular
- **Respiration:** 28/min, shallow
- **Hydration:** 6% dehydration estimated (skin tent slow, mucous membranes tacky)
- **Mentation:** Depressed but responsive; resists handling weakly
- **Right Hindlimb:** Deep laceration, approx. 6 cm × 3 cm, over lateral aspect of tibiotarsal region; muscle visible; moderate ooze; no crepitus or instability on palpation
- **Right Ear:** Small full-thickness tear at pinna edge, approx. 1 cm; dried blood present
- **Thorax/Abdomen:** No external wounds; palpation revealed no crepitus or guarding; heart and lung auscultation clear
- **Neurological:** Pupils equal and responsive; withdrawal reflex present in both forelimbs; diminished but present in right hindlimb
- **Radiographs (lateral and ventrodorsal, pelvis and both hindlimbs):** No fractures or luxations observed. Mild soft tissue swelling around right stifle.

---

**2. PROVISIONAL DIAGNOSIS**

1.  Lacerated wound with muscle involvement, right hindlimb.
2.  Pinna laceration, right ear.
3.  Mild dehydration and hypovolemic shock (early).
4.  Suspected soft tissue contusion, right stifle.

---

**3. TREATMENT PROTOCOL**

Indian Grey Wolf release_date 2024-03-15 date. Record status: historical.

**Day 1 – 2 (12–13/01/2024): Stabilization and Wound Management**

- **Fluids:** Ringer’s Lactate, 500 ml IV, given over 4 hours on Day 1. Repeated at 250 ml IV on Day 2.
- **Antibiotic:** Amoxicillin + Clavulanic acid 500 mg, IV, once daily (SID) for 3 days. *Note: switched to oral after Day 3.*
- **Analgesic:** Meloxicam 0.2 mg/kg, IM, once daily for 3 days.
- **Wound Care:** Copious lavage with sterile normal saline. Debridement of devitalized muscle tissue and skin edges under sedation (Xylazine 1 mg/kg + Ketamine 2 mg/kg IM). Wound left open for drainage. Dressed with sterile gauze soaked in povidone-iodine solution. Bandage changed daily.
- **Ear Wound:** Cleansed with antiseptic solution. No suturing required. Left open to heal by secondary intention.
- **Nutrition:** Not offered on Day 1. Oral rehydration solution (ORS) offered on Day 2; animal lapped small amounts.

**Day 3 – 7 (14–18/01/2024): Wound Healing Phase**

- **Antibiotic:** Amoxicillin + Clavulanic acid 500 mg, PO, BID.
- **Analgesic:** Meloxicam 0.1 mg/kg, PO, SID for 4 more days.
- **Wound Care:** Daily cleaning with dilute chlorhexidine solution (0.05%). Wound granulating well. Serosanguinous discharge minimal. Bandage changed every 48 hours after Day 5.
- **Nutrition:** Started on minced chicken (approx. 500 g/day) mixed with bone meal. Animal eating well from Day 4 onward.
- **Enclosure:** Kept in a quiet, shaded enclosure (size 4 m × 3 m) with visual barrier to reduce stress. Minimal human contact.

**Day 8 – 21 (19/01–01/02/2024): Continued Recovery**

- **Antibiotic:** Stopped after 10 days total (Day 10, 21/01/2024). Wound clean, healthy granulation tissue.
- **Wound Care:** Bandage discontinued on Day 12. Wound left open to air. Daily observation only.
- **Nutrition:** Increased to 800 g minced meat daily. Weight gain noted: 22.1 kg on Day 14, 23.0 kg on Day 21.
- **Activity:** Animal ambulating well, bearing weight on right hindlimb with only a subtle limp. No signs of pain on palpation.

**Day 22 – 40 (02/02–20/02/2024): Pre-release Conditioning**

- **Enclosure:** Moved to a larger pre-release enclosure (10 m × 8 m) with natural substrate, brush piles, and a small water trough.
- **Diet:** Whole carcass feed (goat) provided twice weekly to assess hunting/feeding behavior. Animal fed readily and defended food.
- **Observation:** Behavior noted as alert, wary of humans. No stereotypic pacing. Right hindlimb gait normal. Ear wound healed with a small notch.
- **Weight on Day 40:** 24.2 kg.

In addition, 16 waterhole points were observed for a continuous period of 4 hours each on two consecutive days (11 and 12 December). Observations were made by a team of 28 enumerators, comprising forest staff, research assistants, and local villagers. All enumerators were provided with binoculars and data sheets. GPS coordinates were recorded for every sighting.

The population estimates were derived using the distance sampling method. The software DISTANCE 6.0 was used for analysis. Density estimates were calculated for each species and extrapolated to the total available habitat. The available habitat was taken as 7,400 sq km, which includes the sanctuary, the Banni Grasslands, and the contiguous revenue wasteland.

The census was affected by fog on the morning of 10 December, and the transects scheduled for that morning were completed on 13 December instead. One transect in the Banni area could not be completed due to a vehicle breakdown; this transect was re-walked on 14 December.

**2. Population Estimates**

The population estimates for the major ungulate species and the principal carnivore are given in Table 1 below. The figures are rounded to the nearest ten for all species except the Indian wolf, where the number is given as an approximate range due to the low sample size.

Note: The Chinkara estimate of 1,450 individuals is a historical figure, as recorded in this census report. It is not a current controlled entry and should be treated as the baseline for the year 2023.

**3. Chinkara (Indian Gazelle) Observations**

The Chinkara population was found to be widely distributed across the entire census area. The highest sighting rates were recorded in the Banni Grasslands and the scrublands south of the Kachchh Desert Wildlife Sanctuary. Density was lower in the pure grassland areas of Banni, where the habitat is dominated by tall grass species, and higher in the mixed scrub-grassland ecotone.

During the census, 412 direct sightings of Chinkara were recorded, involving 1,180 individual animals. Group sizes ranged from solitary individuals to a maximum of 14 animals. The average group size was 2.9. Fawns were observed in 22% of the groups, indicating a successful breeding season.

Chinkara were observed drinking at waterholes on 11 occasions. No Chinkara were seen at the waterholes on the second day of observation, which suggests that natural dew and forage moisture may have been sufficient.

DESCRIPTIVE NOTE ON KUTCH WILDLIFE SANCTUARY
(Position as on 01/01/2023)

1. INTRODUCTION AND LEGAL STATUS

Kutch Wildlife Sanctuary is one of the smaller protected areas in the Kachchh district, notified primarily to conserve the arid and semi-arid grassland and scrub ecosystem typical of the region. The sanctuary falls within the jurisdiction of Kutch Wildlife Range, Kachchh (West) Wildlife Division. The final notification under Section 26(A) of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, was issued vide Notification No. WLP/1086/84/1532 dated 11/09/1986. The sanctuary is managed with the primary objective of protecting the chinkara (Indian gazelle) and its habitat, while also providing a secure area for the Indian wolf, desert fox, and various resident and migratory birds.

2. GEOGRAPHICAL LOCATION AND BOUNDARIES

The sanctuary is situated in the western part of Kachchh district, approximately 45 km west of Bhuj town. The area lies between 23°10' N and 23°25' N latitude and 69°30' E and 69°45' E longitude. The sanctuary is bounded on the north by revenue wasteland and scrubland, on the east by agricultural fields of the villages of Nirona and Kotay, on the south by the seasonal riverbed and grazing land, and on the west by the boundary of the adjoining revenue village. The boundary pillars are numbered from KP-1 to KP-118 and are maintained by the Range staff.

The terrain is generally flat to gently undulating, with scattered low hills and depressions. The highest point within the sanctuary is near the central-eastern side, rising to about 150 m above mean sea level. The general slope is towards the south-west, where the drainage converges into a seasonal nullah that flows out of the sanctuary during heavy rainfall years. The soil is predominantly sandy loam with patches of clay in the low-lying areas and gravelly soil on the elevated tracts.

The Division continued its regular patrol regime across the sanctuary and its fringe areas. A total of 1,240 patrol man-days were recorded during the quarter, with an average of 10 patrol parties operating daily. Night patrols were intensified in the areas bordering Nirona and Kotay villages, following reports of suspicious movement.

Two cases of unauthorized grazing were booked under Section 33 of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, and the cattle were impounded at the Range office. The Division attended to 23 rescue calls during the quarter, involving both wild and domestic animals. The details of significant rescues are as follows:

3. On 21/06/2024, a common krait was rescued from a residential compound in Bhuj town by the divisional rescue team. The snake was released in a safe location away from human habitation on the same day.

The remaining 20 rescue calls pertained to birds, including owls, kites, and a painted stork that had suffered wing injuries. All birds received first aid and were either released or transferred to the nearest recognized treatment facility as per protocol.

**Subject: Revised Guidelines for Wildlife Rescue and Rehabilitation Operations – Implementation and Compliance**

In supersession of all previous circulars on the subject, the following comprehensive guidelines are hereby issued for the standardised handling of wildlife rescue, first-aid, transportation, and rehabilitation across all territorial and sanctuary divisions under the Wildlife Circle, Bhuj. These protocols take effect from 1 February 2026, with a mandatory training period for all field staff during the last fortnight of January 2026.

**1. Scope and Applicability**

1.1 These guidelines apply to all forest personnel, including Range Forest Officers (RFOs), Deputy Conservators of Forests (DCFs), veterinary officers, and temporary staff engaged in rescue operations.

1.2 The provisions cover all wild fauna, including reptiles, birds, and mammals, found within the territorial jurisdiction of the Wildlife Circle, Bhuj. They do not apply to domestic livestock or companion animals, which remain under the purview of the District Animal Husbandry Department.

1.3 All rescue operations shall be conducted in accordance with the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, as amended, and the Standing Orders of the Chief Wildlife Warden, Gujarat State.

**2. Reporting and Initial Response**

2.1 Any information regarding a wild animal in distress, conflict, or requiring intervention shall be recorded in the prescribed format (Form R-1) at the nearest Forest Range Office. The form shall be entered in the daily diary maintained at each range.

2.2 Upon receipt of a complaint, the RFO or his designated subordinate shall verify the information within two hours of receipt during daylight hours. For night-time complaints, verification shall commence at first light unless the situation is assessed as an emergency.

2.3 Emergency situations, including but not limited to snakebite incidents, animal attacks on humans, or animals trapped in wells, shall be reported immediately by phone to the Divisional Forest Officer (DFO) and the nearest veterinary officer on duty. The phone report shall be followed by a written report within 24 hours.

2.4 All complaints, whether attended or not, shall be logged in a centralised register at the range level. The register shall be open for inspection by the DCF during all supervisory visits.

**3. Rescue Team Composition and Equipment**

3.1 Each division shall maintain a minimum of one fully equipped rescue kit at the division headquarters and one at each range headquarters. The kit shall include, but not be limited to:

a) Catch poles of varying lengths (6 ft, 10 ft, and 14 ft)
b) Snake tongs and snake tubes (three sizes)
c) Heavy-duty gloves, leather gauntlets, and safety goggles
d) Cloth bags, gunny bags, and ventilated transport crates
e) Ropes, nets, and hooks for well rescues
f) First-aid kit comprising antiseptics, bandages, splints, and saline
g) Torch, headlamps, and spare batteries
h) Mobile phone with emergency contact numbers pre-programmed

3.2 The rescue team shall consist of at least three trained personnel for mammal rescues and at least two trained personnel for reptile rescues. No rescue operation shall be undertaken by a single individual.

3.3 All personnel involved in rescue operations shall undergo a two-day refresher training at the division headquarters once every six months. The first such training under these guidelines shall be completed by 30 June 2026.

documents.title: Field Log - Kachchh Desert Wildlife Rescue and Rehabilitation Centre
documents.content:
01/01/2025, Wednesday
07:15 – Started patrol from Bhuj side, route B-3 towards Jangiya. Sky clear, cold wind from north. No rain last night.
08:40 – Checked waterhole at K-12. Water level low but usable. Filled the trough from tanker.
09:10 – Two chinkara seen near the old babul patch, about 300 m east of K-12. They moved off slowly, not alarmed. I noted them in the sighting register.
11:30 – Back to base. Fuel top-up done. Vehicle rattling noise from rear left, but fine.

02/01/2025, Thursday
06:50 – Early patrol to L-4 and L-5. Mist till 8 AM, then clear.
09:15 – Fresh pugmarks near L-4, likely jackal. No livestock reported missing from nearby villages this week.
11:00 – Repaired fencing near the nursery. Wire was loose at two posts.
13:30 – Took photos of the new solar pump installation for the office file.

03/01/2025, Friday
07:30 – Patrol to M-2. Windy day, dust in patches.
09:00 – Saw a pair of desert fox near the dunes. No chinkara.
10:20 – Checked the camera trap at M-2. Memory card full; replaced with new one. Old card filed in the drawer.
14:00 – Helped Dr. Shah carry the medicine box from the store to the treatment room. Nothing else.

04/01/2025, Saturday
08:10 – Went to village Dhrang for the awareness meeting. Around 25 people attended.
10:00 – Talked about not letting dogs chase chinkara during calving season. Distributed pamphlets.
12:30 – On return, stopped at K-14. No wildlife seen.
15:00 – Office work: updated the vehicle log, filed the camera trap card label.

05/01/2025, Sunday
07:00 – Weekly count route, section C. Started with clear sky.
08:20 – At C-3, three chinkara (two females, one male) near the Prosopis patch. They were alert but did not run.
09:40 – C-5: no large mammals. Some hare tracks.
11:00 – Returned. Weather note: temperature around 18°C at 8 AM, rising to 26°C by noon.

06/01/2025, Monday
07:45 – Patrol to N-1. Overcast, no rain.
09:00 – Found a dead chinkara near the railway line, no visible injury. Probably old age or disease. Took GPS point, informed Dr. Shah. Body removed for post-mortem at the Centre.
11:30 – Dr. Shah said the post-mortem will be done tomorrow. I cleaned the vehicle after carrying the body.

Field observations note Chinkara sighting_frequency_2025 as monthly. Record status: pending verification.

07/01/2025, Tuesday
07:20 – Routine patrol to O-2. Cool morning.
08:50 – No chinkara sighting. Saw a few doves and one hare.
10:00 – Checked the fodder stock at the Centre. Two bales of dry grass remaining; ordered more from the supplier.
13:00 – Assisted with the post-mortem of the chinkara found yesterday. Dr. Shah said it was likely a weak heart. No sign of poisoning.

08/01/2025, Wednesday
06:40 – Early patrol to P-1. Foggy till 7:30.
09:00 – Two chinkara near the salt pan edge, feeding. They stayed for about 10 minutes, then moved north.
10:30 – Checked the fence line near P-1. One post broken by cattle; repaired.
12:00 – Returned. Wrote the sighting note in the register.

09/01/2025, Thursday
07:00 – Patrol to Q-3. Clear sky, light breeze.
08:30 – No chinkara. Saw tracks of a small herd, maybe 4–5 animals, heading east. Could not locate them.
10:00 – Cleaned the water trough at Q-3 and refilled.
11:30 – Back to base. Vehicle fine.

10/01/2025, Friday
07:10 – Patrol to R-2. Windy, dust in the air.
08:45 – One chinkara male near the ridge, standing alert. It moved off when I stopped the vehicle.
09:30 – Checked the camera trap at R-2. No photos of interest.
11:00 – Returned. Updated the daily sheet.

11/01/2025, Saturday
08:00 – Went to village Khavda for a school talk. About 40 children attended.
10:00 – Showed them photos of local wildlife, explained why we should not disturb chinkara during breeding.
12:00 – Back to Centre. No patrol in the afternoon.
